prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with B002 first and B022 second, and having read the eight ballots I now put B022 first. It is the one candidate that six of eight members placed in their top three, and four of them ranked it first on different grounds: Danielsson on discovery, Johansson and Lindroth on control of every systematic, Kroll on the measurement advance. As an instrument builder I judge it on the criteria I use for my own field: a clear idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts for many atoms at once), a patient programme of systematics control (Ye's group taking Sr to the 10^-18 regime and the clock-comparison and laser-stability technology around it), independent reproduction by RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL, and a concrete payoff: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a pending redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize covered earlier steps, so this is a distinct advance. I would take a configuration the committee can defend in one sentence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness and credit. Lattice clocks sit on the frequency-comb (2005) and trapped-ion (2012) lineage, and a sceptic can call them a further precision step instead of a new phenomenon; the discovery content so far is mostly upper limits and consistency tests, with no new effect observed. On credit, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups made decisive contributions to the 10^-18 result, and Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so some of the societal case is prospective. I also note that my own first-ranked candidate, B002, is a single-name credit for a large collaboration, so I am not sure it can be built into a fair prize, which is a reason I moved it down.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B022 first because the discovery is unambiguous, but he asks whether it is sufficiently distinct from the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes, and he ranks IceCube (B002) fifth, with doubts about the one-name credit and the 3 to 4 sigma source associations.
responses.response: I agree with both points and they change my ranking. On distinctness, the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured single-ion control; the lattice clock is a different technical route (many atoms, magic wavelength, a quantum-many-body clock) with a different error budget, so I think the distinction can be written into the citation. On IceCube you are right that the diffuse flux is solid but individual sources, TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068, are still at modest significance and a one-person award for a large collaboration is delicate. I still think neutrino astronomy will deserve a prize, but I no longer think it is ready to carry this year.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first as precise, interpretable atomic physics, and she warns that a prize in B020 interacts with the related B035/B036 candidates and that Chu's absence complicates B004. She is more cautious on astrophysics such as B002.
responses.response: As an outsider to atomic physics I rely on your judgement of the error budgets, and it matches what I would check as a detector person: independent reproduction and comparison of clocks over fibre links. Your caution on the astrophysics candidates is fair, and I accept that I cannot expect atomic colleagues to rank B002 highly when attribution is a single name. I do press you on one point: if you think the two-name B022 credit is natural, I would like to hear whether you would insist on adding anyone, since I would resist widening it to dilute a clean prize.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B038 (tunnel magnetoresistance) first as an original experiment with large technological consequence, but she ranks B022 third and notes the credit for the MgO part sits partly with people outside the list and that the 2007 GMR prize must be distinguished.
responses.response: I respect the experimental case for B038 and I like the idea that a verified effect can be traced into read heads and MRAM. My reservation is that you yourself identify that the third credited name is arguable and that Yuasa and Djayaprawira are missing, so a three-person prize would leave out the people who delivered the giant MgO effect, while the 1995 discovery alone overlaps with the GMR prize. B022 has no equivalent attribution hole. I would keep B038 as a serious later candidate but I do not think it is ready as a fair configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B018 (dynamical mean-field theory) first as overdue and tied to materials via DFT+DMFT, and ranks B038 and B028 next, while giving B022 no place in his top eight.
responses.response: I cannot judge the DMFT work in detail and I rely on you for that. But my question as Chair is whether the credit can be written down. You say yourself that Metzner is a real omission from the trio, and that is a structural difficulty, not a footnote: the committee would be recognising a framework while excluding one of its originators. Mehlig also calls it an approximation scheme rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon. I take your point that it is overdue, but I would want that attribution question resolved before I support it over a candidate whose names are clear.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B022 first and B020 second, and proposes Bloch, Cirac and Zoller for B020 with a theory-heavy credit that leaves out Greiner and Esslinger; he has also declared his closeness to B014.
responses.response: I appreciate that you declare your closeness to circuit QED, and I agree it is right to weigh that. On B020 I agree it is the best second candidate on the shortlist, and the allocation is the hard part: your trio favours theory, Danielsson, Lindroth and I propose Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, and Kroll adds Esslinger. Until we agree on which names are decisive, I would keep B020 as the principal alternative and not a joint prize with B022.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether credit should be limited to Katori and Ye given the large JILA team and the contributions of the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups; I have no way to verify the allocation beyond the shortlist.
Whether a second prize part (for example B020 or B002) should share the prize, which depends on whether the committee can agree on a clean three-name credit for it.
Eriksson's and Olsson's condensed-matter judgement on B018 and B038 is outside my expertise and I have not been able to test the credit arguments independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B022. For disclosure: my own field is astroparticle physics and I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations; I ranked B002 (IceCube) and B009 (kilonovae) in a neighbouring field, but I have no known personal or institutional tie to IceCube or its credited candidate, and I will take the field closeness into account when weighing them.
